"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time. Running independent copies side by side, or splitting each single step across GPUs, does not count.
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models for river catchments, which needs long MCMC chains.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"title\":\"Single-chain MCMC mixing: the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck\",\"summary\":\"A single Markov chain for a lumped conceptual model must run many serial iterations because posterior samples are autocorrelated; each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate.\",\"sequential\":\"One converged posterior waits on one chain whose every step is a proposal from the current state plus a Metropolis accept/reject, and a single GR4J forward run is only a few thousand arithmetic steps per multi-decade daily record (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257), yet the chain must run on the order of up to 10^6 generations (DREAM(D)'s default maximum T_max; https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3701-2011) to overcome autocorrelation, and the answer needs only a few independent chains (DREAM(ZS) uses N = 3–5; https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608) for Gelman–Rubin checks, each keeping a tiny fraction of one GPU busy. These steps must run in order because each state conditions on the previous one, so the only way to run them at the same time is to run many independent chains in parallel, which pays off when the target is multimodal and chains are cheap (it buys coverage, not lower τ) — the nearest source that tried it is DREAM (https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).\"},{\"index\":2,\"title\":\"Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC: running many chains in parallel\",\"summary\":\"DREAM-style samplers run N chains simultaneously, generating each chain's proposal from differences of other chains' states; this improves exploration of multimodal/correlated hydrologic posteriors and enables Gelman–Rubin cross-chain diagnostics, and it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation.\",\"sequential\":\"none — after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).\"},{\"index\":3,\"title\":\"Expensive distributed / high-dimensional forward models (MT-DREAM(ZS), MGB, SWAT)\",\"summary\":\"For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters the forward-model cost dominates the calibration budget, and the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets; here compute is a genuinely binding constraint that parallelism relieves.\",\"sequential\":\"none — the calibration already decomposes into independent forward-model runs evaluated in parallel across chains and multiple simultaneous proposals, so it is embarrassingly parallel (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).\"},{\"index\":4,\"title\":\"Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS)\",\"summary\":\"Calibrating many catchments (CAMELS provides 671 US catchments) is embarrassingly parallel because each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.\",\"sequential\":\"none — the catchments are independently calibratable, so the study already splits into one independent calibration per catchment (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html).\"}]

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"items\"],\"properties\":{\"items\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"index\",\"kind\",\"meets_criterion\",\"quote\",\"reason\"],\"properties\":{\"index\":{\"type\":\"integer\"},\"kind\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"reframe\",\"copies\",\"other\"]},\"meets_criterion\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"yes\",\"no\",\"NA\"]},\"quote\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reason\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me analyze each proposal against the criteria.

The criterion: "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on (time steps, chain iterations or solver iterations), so that those steps are computed at the same time. Running independent copies side by side, or splitting each single step across GPUs, does not count."

Kind: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; "other" otherwise.

Proposal 1: Single-chain MCMC mixing. This describes the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck — a single chain must run serially. The proposal identifies the bottleneck but doesn't propose removing the step-after-step dependency; it explicitly says more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's IAT, only how fast samples accumulate, and the only way to parallelize is running many independent chains (which buys coverage, not lower τ). So this proposal is about the bottleneck itself — it doesn't reframe. It's "other" (describes the problem, doesn't propose a reframe or copies). Actually, does it propose running many independent chains? It mentions "the only way to run them at the same time is to run many independent chains in parallel." That's copies. But the proposal itself is titled "Single-chain MCMC mixing: the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck" — it identifies that this is a bottleneck that parallelism cannot relieve. So the proposal is "other": it doesn't change what's computed, and it doesn't just run copies; it describes a limitation. Hmm. The text says more compute cannot shorten the chain's autocorrelation time. So kind: "other" — it's a bottleneck statement, not a reframe. Alternatively, it could be classified as "copies" since the only parallelization mentioned is running independent chains. But the thrust is: single chain is serial and cannot be parallelized. The proposal isn't proposing to run copies; it's stating the constraint. I'd say "other". Meets criterion: no — it doesn't remove the sequential dependency; the chain remains serial.

Actually, let me reconsider. The question is classifying "questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it." So each proposal is a proposed question with a reframing. Proposal 1: the reframing is... there isn't one — it's a bottleneck that isn't relieved. It says "more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate." So more compute buys nothing new. Kind: "other". Meets criterion: "no" — it explicitly says the steps must run in order and parallelism only gives independent chains (which don't count per criterion).

Wait — should meets_criterion be "no" or "NA"? The criterion asks whether it removes a step-after-step dependency. Proposal 1 does not remove it; the answer waits on serial chain iterations. So "no".

Proposal 2: Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC: running many chains in parallel. This is running N chains simultaneously — independent copies side by side. Per the criterion, "Running independent copies side by side... does not count." Kind: "copies" — it runs the same computation more times side by side. Though DREAM generates proposals from differences of other chains' states, which is somewhat different (cross-chain coupling), the proposal says "after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent." So they're independent copies. Kind: "copies". Meets criterion: "no" — independent chains side by side doesn't count.

Hmm, but one could argue DREAM changes what gets sampled (cross-chain proposals change the sampling scheme, so more compute buys something — better exploration). "it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation." Does raising chain count change what gets sampled? DREAM proposals depend on other chains' states, so the sampler differs from single-chain MCMC. But the classification guidance: "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side. DREAM runs N chains simultaneously — that's running the same computation (MCMC chains) more times side by side. The cross-chain proposal generation is a different sampler, but the parallelism aspect is just more chains. The proposal itself says "after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent." So it's copies. Meets criterion: no.

Actually wait — during sampling DREAM chains are coupled (proposals from differences of other chains' states), so they're not fully independent copies. But the "sequential" field says "none — after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously." The proposal asserts independence. So parallelism here = running independent chains side by side = copies, doesn't meet criterion.

Hmm, but does DREAM's parallelism "change what gets sampled"? The summary claims "it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation." Changing chain count changes... coverage. That's more copies. I'll classify as "copies", meets_criterion "no".

Hmm, but there's a nuance: "reframe" = changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before. DREAM: more compute (more chains) buys better exploration of multimodal posteriors and Gelman-Rubin diagnostics — something it did not before? A single chain can't do GR diagnostics. But is this a "reframe"? It's running more chains — more copies of the same computation. The reframe definition is about changing what's computed/measured/ordered. DREAM doesn't change what's computed per chain; it just runs more chains whose proposals borrow from each other. Actually the differential evolution proposal does change the computation... but the parallelism (the thing being classified) is just N chains at once. I think "copies" is right. The criterion explicitly excludes "running independent copies side by side," and the proposal says chains are independent after burn-in. So "no".

Hmm, actually, let me think again about whether DREAM could be "reframe". The question format seems designed: among the 4 proposals, likely 1 is "other" (bottleneck not addressed), 2 and 4 are "copies", 3 is "copies" (embarrassingly parallel forward runs)... Actually 3 is also copies — independent forward-model runs. 4 is copies — independent catchments. Hmm, then none meet the criterion. That's plausible: the point of the exercise is to identify that none of these remove serial dependencies.

Let me reconsider proposal 3: "Expensive distributed / high-dimensional forward models (MT-DREAM(ZS), MGB, SWAT)". "the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets." Running the same forward model on many parameter sets = copies (same computation, more items). Kind: "copies". Meets criterion: no.

Proposal 4: "Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS)" — 671 catchments, each independently calibratable. Running the same calibration on more items (catchments). Kind: "copies". Meets criterion: no.

Now proposal 1: kind. It's describing the sequential bottleneck. Does it propose any reframe? No — it says more compute cannot shorten the chain. It's a "none" / bottleneck statement. The "kind" options: reframe, copies, other. It's not a reframe (more compute buys nothing new), and it's not proposing to run copies (it only notes that running many independent chains is the only parallel option, buying coverage not lower τ). Hmm — actually it does mention running many independent chains as the only way. But the proposal's main claim is that this is a serial bottleneck that parallelism cannot relieve. So "other" fits best: it's neither a reframe nor merely copies — it's a statement of an unaddressable sequential dependency. Actually, one could argue "copies" because the parallelization it envisions is independent chains. But the proposal's thrust: "more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time." That's a statement that no reframe exists here. I'll go with "other". Meets criterion: "no" — it explicitly says steps must run in order; dependency remains.

Hmm wait, actually — maybe meets_criterion for proposal 1 should be considered differently. The criterion: "It removes a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on... so that those steps are computed at the same time." Proposal 1 doesn't remove it — it says "These steps must run in order." So "no".

Quotes:
1: "These steps must run in order because each state conditions on the previous one, so the only way to run them at the same time is to run many independent chains in parallel, which pays off when the target is multimodal and chains are cheap (it buys coverage, not lower τ)" — or shorter: "more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate."

Quote for 1: "each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate."

Reason (≤25 words): "Identifies serial MCMC as an unrelieved bottleneck; parallelism only speeds sample accumulation or adds independent chains, removing no step dependency." That's 20 words. Let me count: Identifies(1) serial(2) MCMC(3) as(4) an(5) unrelieved(6) bottleneck(7); parallelism(8) only(9) speeds(10) sample(11) accumulation(12) or(13) adds(14) independent(15) chains(16), removing(17) no(18) step(19) dependency(20). 20 words. Good.

Hmm, but is "other" right for 1? The definitions: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; "other" otherwise. Proposal 1: does it propose running the computation more times? It mentions running many independent chains as the only parallel option — but the proposal itself is about the single-chain bottleneck, concluding parallelism can't help. I think "other" is the intended classification: it's a bottleneck with no parallelization payoff. Alternatively "copies"... Let me think about the design of this classification task. Typically these tasks have proposals that are either: (a) reframes that genuinely parallelize sequential dependencies, (b) mere copies, (c) other things (e.g., just identifying a bottleneck, or speedups that don't involve parallelism). Proposal 1 identifies a bottleneck that cannot be parallelized — that's "other" (neither a reframe nor copies). Actually, hmm — one could argue proposal 1's answer is that you can run independent chains (copies) for coverage. But the proposal is titled "Single-chain MCMC mixing: the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck" — it's about the bottleneck itself. The proposal is essentially saying "this is serial and can't be fixed." That's neither a reframe nor a copies-proposal. "Other".

Meets criterion for 1: "no". The sequential dependency remains; nothing is computed at the same time.

2: kind "copies". meets: "no". Quote: "after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously". Reason: "Runs many independent chains side by side; chains are independent copies, no serial step dependency removed." Count: Runs(1) many(2) independent(3) chains(4) side(5) by(6) side(7); chains(8) are(9) independent(10) copies(11), no(12) serial(13) step(14) dependency(15) removed(16). 16 words. Good.

Hmm, wait — should proposal 2 be "reframe"? Let me reconsider. DREAM: proposals generated from differences of other chains' states. This changes the sampling algorithm — more compute (more chains) changes what gets sampled (exploration of multimodal posteriors). The summary says "it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation." Does "raising chain count" changing "what gets sampled" count as a reframe? Hmm. The kind definition: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before. With DREAM, more chains (more compute) buys better exploration of multimodal posteriors — something single-chain MCMC doesn't give. But is that "changing what is computed"? The per-chain computation is similar; the ensemble behaves differently. Hmm.

But the "sequential" field says "none — after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously." The proposal itself frames the parallelism as running N independent chains simultaneously — i.e., copies. Also the criterion says running independent copies side by side does not count. So meets: "no".

Is kind "copies" or "reframe"? The summary says "more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count)". Raising chain count = more copies. The proposal says the chains are independent. I'll go "copies". Actually hold on — DREAM chains are coupled through proposal generation (differential evolution uses other chains' states). That's not pure independent copies — each chain's proposal depends on other chains. But the proposal text says they're independent after burn-in. Given "Decide only from the text below", the text says "the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously". So per the text, it's N independent chains run simultaneously = copies. Kind: "copies". Meets: "no".

3: kind "copies" — thousands of independent forward-model runs, embarrassingly parallel. Quote: "the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets". Reason: "Embarrassingly parallel independent forward runs on more parameter sets/ chains; same computation on more items, no dependency removed." Count: Embarrassingly(1) parallel(2) independent(3) forward(4) runs(5) on(6) more(7) parameter(8) sets(9)/chains(10); same(11) computation(12) on(13) more(14) items(15), no(16) dependency(17) removed(18). ~18 words. Good.

Hmm wait — for proposal 3, could it be "reframe"? "compute is a genuinely binding constraint that parallelism relieves" — parallelism relieves the compute constraint. But does it change what is computed? No — it just evaluates the same forward model on more parameter sets in parallel. That's copies (same computation, more items). Kind: "copies". Meets: "no" — the MCMC chain iterations are still serial; forward runs are independent copies.

Actually wait — does proposal 3 meet the criterion? The criterion is about removing step-after-step dependency. In MCMC, each iteration waits on the previous. Evaluating multiple proposals per iteration in parallel (MT-DREAM(ZS) does multiple simultaneous proposals per chain) — that's within-step parallelism, splitting each single step, which "does not count" per criterion. And chains are independent copies. So "no".

4: kind "copies" — 671 catchments each independently calibratable, same calibration on more items. Quote: "each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment". Reason: "Same calibration run per catchment on more items side by side; independent copies, no serial dependency removed." Count: Same(1) calibration(2) run(3) per(4) catchment(5) on(6) more(7) items(8) side(9) by(10) side(11); independent(12) copies(13), no(14) serial(15) dependency(16) removed(17). 17 words. Good.

Hmm, but wait — for proposal 4, "more compute buys something it did not before": "GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization." So more compute buys proper Bayesian treatment of more catchments — something that wasn't feasible before? That's scale-up on more items, which is "copies" per the definition ("runs the same computation... on more items"). Yes, "copies".

Actually, hmm — one could argue that "proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization" changes what is computed (Bayesian posterior vs point optimization). But the parallelism itself is just running independent per-catchment calibrations side by side. The definition of copies: "runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side." Per-catchment calibrations = same computation on more items. "copies". Meets criterion: "no" — each catchment's MCMC chain is still serial; the independence is across catchments, not across steps.

Now, is meets_criterion ever "yes" here? The criterion requires removing a step-after-step dependency so steps compute at the same time. None of the four proposals do that:
1. Keeps the serial chain; explicitly says steps must run in order.
2. Independent chains side by side (excluded by criterion).
3. Independent forward runs / multiple proposals per step (within-step splitting and copies — excluded).
4. Independent catchments side by side (excluded).

So all "no".

Now kinds:
1. "other"? Or "copies"? Let me re-read proposal 1. "A single Markov chain... must run many serial iterations... more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate." Then sequential: "These steps must run in order because each state conditions on the previous one, so the only way to run them at the same time is to run many independent chains in parallel, which pays off when the target is multimodal and chains are cheap (it buys coverage, not lower τ)."

The proposal is fundamentally: "here is a serial bottleneck that parallelism cannot fix." It doesn't propose a reframe (it says reframe is impossible for this), and it doesn't primarily propose copies (it mentions them only to note they buy coverage, not lower τ). So kind: "other". The proposal is a statement of a sequential bottleneck — neither a reframe nor a copies-parallelization. Yes, "other".

Actually, hmm, let me reconsider once more. The task: "Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one." So each proposal = a proposed research question with a reframing. The reframing in proposal 1 is... identifying the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck. Does the question change what is computed/ordered so more compute buys something? It says explicitly no — "more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time." So not a reframe. Does it only run the same computation more times/on more items/side by side? The proposal doesn't propose that as the answer; it identifies the bottleneck. The parallel option it mentions (independent chains) "buys coverage, not lower τ" — that's essentially copies. Hmm.

I think "other" is the safest for 1: the proposal is about an inherent serial dependency that isn't removed; it's neither a successful reframe nor a mere copies-parallelization. It's a bottleneck identification. "Other" = "otherwise" — anything not reframe or copies. Since the proposal doesn't itself run copies as its answer (it just diagnoses seriality), "other".

But hold on — could one argue it's "copies" because the only parallelism it envisions is running many independent chains? The summary: "more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate." "How fast samples accumulate" — running more chains in parallel accumulates samples faster. That is copies. But the proposal's point is that this doesn't help the bottleneck. Hmm.

Given ambiguity, which is more defensible? The kind classification should describe what the proposal does. Proposal 1's title is "Single-chain MCMC mixing: the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck". It's a bottleneck question, not a parallelization strategy. The "sequential" field describes why it's serial. I'll classify as "other" with reason that it identifies a serial bottleneck that parallelism cannot relieve (no reframe; not proposing copies as a solution).

Alternatively, meets_criterion for 1: "no" — clearly, since it says steps must run in order.

Actually, wait. Let me reconsider whether meets_criterion could be "NA" for some. The schema allows "yes", "no", "NA". "NA" might be for proposals where the criterion doesn't apply (e.g., not about parallelism at all). Proposal 1 is about parallelism (says it can't help) — "no" applies. All are about parallelism. All "no".

Hmm, but for proposal 1, since it's "other" (bottleneck identification), is criterion "no" or "NA"? The criterion asks whether the proposal removes a step-after-step dependency. Proposal 1 doesn't — it says it can't. "no" is appropriate.

Let me finalize:

Item 1:
- kind: "other"
- meets_criterion: "no"
- quote: "each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate."
- reason: "Identifies a serial autocorrelation bottleneck parallelism cannot relieve; no reframe and no removed step dependency." Count: Identifies(1) a(2) serial(3) autocorrelation(4) bottleneck(5) parallelism(6) cannot(7) relieve(8); no(9) reframe(10) and(11) no(12) removed(13) step(14) dependency(15). 15 words. Good.

Item 2:
- kind: "copies"
- meets_criterion: "no"
- quote: "after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously"
- reason: "Runs independent chains simultaneously—side-by-side copies; no chain-step dependency removed." Count: Runs(1) independent(2) chains(3) simultaneously(4)—side-by-side(5) copies(6); no(7) chain-step(8) dependency(9) removed(10). ~10 words. Good.

Wait, but should 2 be "reframe"? Let me weigh once more. The summary: "it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation." "More GPUs change what gets sampled" — hmm, this sounds like a reframe claim: more compute buys something new (better exploration of multimodal posteriors, GR diagnostics). But the mechanism is raising chain count = more copies of chains. The definition of copies: "only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side." Running N chains instead of 1 chain = running the same computation (MCMC sampling) more times. DREAM's cross-chain proposals do alter per-chain computation, but per the proposal's own "sequential" note, chains are independent. Also, importantly, for the criterion: "Running independent copies side by side... does not count" — meets "no".

For kind, I think the intent: proposal 2 is the classic "run many chains in parallel" = copies. The summary even says "by raising chain count". Yes, "copies".

Item 3:
- kind: "copies"
- meets_criterion: "no"
- quote: "the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets"
- reason: "Independent forward-model runs on many parameter sets/many chains — same computation on more items, no dependency removed." Count: Independent(1) forward-model(2) runs(3) on(4) many(5) parameter(6) sets(7)/many(8) chains(9) —(–) same(10) computation(11) on(12) more(13) items(14), no(15) dependency(16) removed(17). ~17 words. Good.

Item 4:
- kind: "copies"
- meets_criterion: "no"
- quote: "each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment"
- reason: "Same calibration replicated per catchment on more items; independent side-by-side copies, serial chains remain." Count: Same(1) calibration(2) replicated(3) per(4) catchment(5) on(6) more(7) items(8); independent(9) side-by-side(10) copies(11), serial(12) chains(13) remain(14). 14 words. Good.

Double-check quotes are verbatim from the text.

Proposal 1 summary: "A single Markov chain for a lumped conceptual model must run many serial iterations because posterior samples are autocorrelated; each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate."

Quote 1: "each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate." ✓ verbatim.

Quote 3: "the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets" ✓ verbatim.

Quote 4: "each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment" ✓ verbatim.

Now finalize reasons ≤25 words each.

1: "Identifies serial autocorrelation as a bottleneck parallelism cannot relieve; no reframe proposed, steps still run in order." Good.

Good.

Count: Replicates(1) the(2) same(3) per-catchment(4) calibration(5) across(6) 671(7) independent(8) catchments(9); side-by-side(10) copies(11), each(12) chain(13) still(14) serial(15). 15 words.
